title: Java HashSet
learningObjectives: Create a HashSet with a generic element type.
Add values and recognize duplicate suppression.
Traverse a set without assuming an order.
Use the Set interface and select HashSet, LinkedHashSet or TreeSet according to uniqueness and ordering requirements.

understand.concept: HashSet implements Set and stores unique elements. Adding an element that is already present does not create a duplicate. HashSet uses hashing for efficient membership checks in typical cases and does not guarantee iteration order. It permits one null element. Use Set when uniqueness is part of the requirement; use a List when order, duplicates or indexed access matter.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic helps Java developers select and use the right standard-library tools for java hashset in maintainable applications.
understand.analogy: Think of the collection or date API as a purpose-built tool: its operations communicate the guarantees your program can rely on.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a guide; Java API contracts, equality rules and exception behaviour determine the actual result.

explain.narrative:
Create a HashSet with a type such as HashSet<String>. add returns true only when the set changes. contains tests membership and remove deletes a value. Iteration order is unspecified, so avoid tests or output that depend on a particular order. For custom elements, implement equals and hashCode consistently so logically equal values are treated as duplicates.

## The Set interface and implementations

`Set<E>` represents unique elements and does not provide positional indexing. `HashSet` makes no iteration-order guarantee. `LinkedHashSet` preserves insertion order. `TreeSet` keeps elements sorted according to natural ordering or a Comparator. Declare a variable as `Set<E>` when the code needs only uniqueness and membership operations, then select the implementation according to ordering requirements.

examples.title: Add unique values
examples.code:
import java.util.HashSet;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashSet<String> tags = new HashSet<>(); tags.add("java"); tags.add("code"); tags.add("java"); System.out.println(tags.size()); } }
examples.explanation: A repeated equal element does not increase the set size.

examples.title: Check membership
examples.code:
import java.util.HashSet;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashSet<Integer> ids = new HashSet<>(); ids.add(10); ids.add(20); System.out.println(ids.contains(20)); System.out.println(ids.contains(30)); } }
examples.explanation: contains tests whether an equal element is present.

examples.title: Remove an element
examples.code:
import java.util.HashSet;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashSet<String> roles = new HashSet<>(); roles.add("reader"); roles.add("editor"); roles.remove("reader"); System.out.println(roles.contains("reader")); } }
examples.explanation: remove deletes the matching element when it exists.

examples.title: Use add result
examples.code:
import java.util.HashSet;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashSet<String> seen = new HashSet<>(); System.out.println(seen.add("A")); System.out.println(seen.add("A")); } }
examples.explanation: add reports whether a new element was inserted.

examples.title: Use Set with LinkedHashSet
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedHashSet; import java.util.Set;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Set<String> tags = new LinkedHashSet<>(); tags.add("java"); tags.add("sql"); tags.add("web"); for (String tag : tags) System.out.println(tag); } }
examples.explanation: Set expresses uniqueness while LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order. TreeSet sorts values, whereas HashSet makes no iteration-order promise.

practise.guidedTask: Declare Set<String> backed by HashSet and add duplicate values. Then use LinkedHashSet to preserve insertion order and TreeSet to sort values. Explain which guarantees belong to Set and which are implementation-specific.
practise.independentTask: Create a registration system that stores unique email-like identifiers. Test duplicate insertion and membership, then print results using LinkedHashSet so the example has deterministic order.
hints: HashSet enforces uniqueness using equals and hashCode; equal values do not create separate set elements.
HashSet does not guarantee iteration order; use LinkedHashSet for insertion order or TreeSet for sorted order.
Test equal-but-distinct objects and keep fields used by equals/hashCode stable while values are stored in the set.
practise.challenge: Explain why Set has no positional indexing. Compare HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet in uniqueness, encounter order and sorting, and describe what a custom element needs for reliable duplicate detection.

questions.prompt: What is the defining property of a Set?
questions.explanation: Set models membership with unique elements.

questions.prompt: What happens when the same value is added twice to HashSet?
questions.answer: The second add does not create another element

questions.prompt: What does add return when an element is already present?
questions.explanation: add returns false when the set is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which Set implementation preserves insertion order?
